rationales.A: The war grew from land: English towns, fences, and cattle kept spreading onto Wampanoag ground, trampling cornfields and crowding out hunting. Metacom — called King Philip by the English — watched his people's land shrink year by year, and by 1675 there was nowhere left to retreat. The Sassamon trial lit the fuse, but the powder was decades of English expansion, and that is why the war began when it did.
rationales.B: The Sassamon trial was the spark, not the underlying cause — the land pressure came first.
rationales.C: No French agents supplied the Wampanoag; the war was an English–Native conflict.
rationales.D: No Spanish missionaries operated in New England.
rationales.general:
1. Separate the spark from the cause. Background: the Sassamon trial lit the fuse in 1675.
2. Ask what the fuse was laid in. Background: decades of English towns, fences, and cattle spreading onto Wampanoag ground.
3. Name the cause. Land pressure — the slow loss of the ground a people lived on.
Remember: a spark explains when a war starts, not why — look for what was building underneath.

stimulus.text: An engraving by F. O. C. Darley, published in 1886 and captioned “The King Philip War — A Raid on the Settlers.” Native warriors carrying tomahawks and clubs attack settlers in a field; one settler fires a musket, a frightened child stands in the center, and a fallen settler lies in the foreground.
